https://www.dw.com/en/belgium-hundreds-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ItqE The blaze is described as by officials as the largest in Belgium's modern history Image: Laurent Cavenati/Belga/AFP Advertisement Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares in the eastern High Fens nature reserve near the German border. On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control . Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area. Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO "You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency. A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter. How have firefighting efforts fared? The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction. Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP "There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said. Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux. Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands. Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area. Climate change making wildfires spread faster Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat this week , with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country. Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer. European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent. "Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said. The wildfire is located just over the border from another major blaze in western Germany , which forced more than 2,000 residents from their homes. https://instinctmagazine.com/lgbtq-stude.text: There is apparently a new way to say “we see you” to LGBTQ+ students at a Catholic high school in Oakland — and it involves a very colorful letter O. RELATED: Poland Rejects Recognition of Foreign Same-Sex Marriages Source: New Ways Ministry Bishop O’Dowd Catholic High School is heading into the new school year without the Pride and Progress flags that had appeared on campus. In their place is the Inclusive O , a rainbow-colored version of the school’s official logo designed to signal that LGBTQ+ students belong, too. Yes, it is technically a logo. Yes, it is also rainbow. And yes, the whole thing has prompted exactly the sort of debate you might expect when a Pride flag meets a Catholic school, a bishop and a community trying very hard to agree on what inclusion should look like. RELATED: Fresno Church’s Rainbow Doors Smashed for a Second Time This Summer The rainbow is staying. Just in a different font, basically. The Inclusive O takes the school’s familiar angular letter and fills it with watercolor-like rainbow shades. KRON-4 described the design this way: “The symbol, an angular, oblong capital ‘O,’ features a smudge of colors, some of which — red, orange, yellow, green, violet, and blue — are also found in the Pride flag. However, rather than the neat, delineated lines of the Pride flag, the colors in the O look more like an impressionist watercolor of leaves.” The school’s own explanation is considerably more direct: “Our Inclusive O was created by and for the O’Dowd community. Using rainbow watercolor in our official O logo, it is underscored by words seen. known. loved.” So, if you were hoping the rainbow itself had been banished from campus, surprise: it has simply been given a school-branded rebrand. The school says the Inclusive O is now displayed campus-wide, replacing the Pride and Progress flags that had previously appeared in some classrooms. What happened to the Pride flags? This is where things get considerably less cute than a watercolor O. In a letter to the school community, president Kim Walsh explained that Pride and Progress flags had become part of a much larger conversation surrounding Catholic schools and LGBTQ+ inclusion. “Many of you know that over the last few years, questions about Pride and Progress flags have become part of a much larger conversation taking place throughout the Catholic Church and in the United States. “Across the country, Catholic schools have been working to navigate these tensions while remaining united as communities, caring for students, and living their catholic values. Last year, this became a lightning rod within our community. We did not want a symbol to become the source of division that diminished our ability to care for students. “Our Inclusive O now appears in lieu of the Pride and Progress flags that had previously been displayed in some classrooms, and is now displayed campus-wide.” Walsh did not identify the specific incident in that letter. Reporting from KQED said the Diocese of Oakland asked the school to remove the Pride flags after someone in the community saw a Progress flag on campus and reported it to Bishop Michael Barber. The school did not immediately comply. Before summer break, however, the flags were removed and featured in a ceremony at the school chapel, while the Inclusive O began appearing on posters and shirts. In other words, the argument over a flag did not exactly disappear. It evolved into a discussion about what should replace it. A year of figuring out what “belonging” looks like The school says the Inclusive O was not dreamed up as a quick compromise after everyone got tired of arguing. Walsh said the school spent months involving faculty, staff, counselors, parents, students, LGBTQ+ community members and others in the process. “Over many months, we engaged faculty and staff, counselors, parents, the Board of Regents, LGBTQ+ community members, and student leaders in prayer, discernment, and dialogue. Together, we asked a simple but important question: How do we continue to visibly communicate that every student belongs?” That question produced a symbol that is unmistakably tied to O’Dowd itself rather than the broader LGBTQ+ movement. And therein lies the interesting part. A Pride flag comes with decades of history and an instantly recognizable message. The Inclusive O comes with a school logo, a rainbow palette and a sentence explaining what it means. For some people, that distinction is the entire point. For others, it is the problem. LGBTQ+ support goes beyond one piece of fabric O’Dowd insists that changing the symbols on the walls does not mean changing its broader support for LGBTQ+ students. Walsh pointed to programs including the school’s Counseling Department, Health & Wellness team, Unity Club, Pride Arts Club and Inclusive Family Day. She also said the school was expanding its efforts this year. “Our Counseling Department, Health & Wellness team, Unity Club, Pride Arts Club, Inclusive Family Day, and the many ways we accompany LGBTQ+ students and families remain in place. This year, we are also expanding that work through a community art workshop, an LGBTQ+ family retreat, and the formation of an Inclusive Advisory Council to help guide our ongoing efforts around belonging and student support.” That is important context because the controversy isn’t simply about whether a rainbow exists somewhere on campus. It is about representation — and whether a school-created symbol can carry the same emotional and cultural weight as the Pride flag it replaces. Some alumni aren’t exactly sending the O a standing ovation Not everyone thinks the new symbol is an adequate substitute. Bishop O’Dowd High School / Source: odowddragons Some alumni have argued that the Inclusive O does not carry the same significance as the Pride flag, which has long been associated with LGBTQ+ visibility. The concern is fairly straightforward: a Pride flag doesn’t need a user manual. One social media post discussed on Reddit said the decision: “‘directly affects the LGBTQ+ population of the school by removing pieces of representation.’” That criticism has become one of the central questions surrounding the change: if the goal is to make LGBTQ+ students feel seen, does replacing a universally recognizable LGBTQ+ symbol with an institution-specific one make that visibility stronger — or harder to recognize? There is no universally agreed answer. One LGBTQ+ advocate thinks the O is a win Francis DeBernardo, executive director of New Ways Ministry, takes a more favorable view. “The new symbol is a positive way to solve a dilemma that many Catholic schools face in regard to Pride flags,” he said. “It is a creative solution that sends a message of support to LGBTQ+ students, and that is the most important feature of it.” And that may be the most charitable way to read what O’Dowd is attempting. The school isn’t pretending the controversy never happened. Instead, it has chosen a symbol it can control, define and put everywhere — one that the administration says communicates belonging without turning the campus into another battleground over the Pride flag. Whether students and alumni ultimately see the Inclusive O as meaningful representation or as a conspicuously school-approved substitute is another question. Because sometimes the symbol is the whole conversation There is something almost perfectly modern about the situation: a community spends a year debating how to communicate inclusion, removes one symbol, creates another, and then finds itself debating the new symbol. But the argument matters because symbols matter. For LGBTQ+ students, seeing a rainbow flag can mean more than decoration. It can be a small but unmistakable signal that someone thought about them before they walked through the door. At the same time, O’Dowd says it wants to avoid allowing that symbol to become a source of division that overshadows its ability to support students. The Inclusive O is therefore doing a lot of work for one letter. It has to be a logo, a compromise, a rainbow, a reassurance and, apparently, a diplomatic envoy. Whether it succeeds may depend less on how pretty the O looks and more on what LGBTQ+ students actually experience once they are inside it. For now, Bishop O’Dowd’s message is clear: the Pride flags are gone, but the school wants its LGBTQ+ students to know that “seen. known. loved.” is still very much the assignment. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-futur.text: Former British chancellor Rachel Reeves has stated that the U.K.’s future should be in the European Union, arguing Brexit has been bad for Britain. Writing in the Sunday Times, Reeves, who was sacked as chancellor by Prime Minister Andy Burnham when he entered Downing Street, said: “I am proud of the progress we have already made in strengthening our relationship with the European Union. Brexit has made us poorer, weaker and less secure. “There is a debate to be had about our future relationship with Europe, and I welcome Andy Burnham’s leadership in facing up to this. No one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were.” Advertisement Advertisement Reeves added that while she believes “Britain’s future lies in the European Union”, it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right.” Last week, Burnham expressed an openness to restarting free movement between the U.K and the EU. He also said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament. At the last election, Labour’s manifesto — which Reeves helped to draw up — said a Labour government would stay outside the EU. But at the Labour Party’s conference in September, Burnham called for closer links with the bloc. Reeves’ intervention comes ahead of a leaders’ summit later this month where she said “at a minimum” she hoped to see confirmation of a youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for. At the Nov. 20 summit, the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/australian-teen-fo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PMPm Prefer DW on Google 'I'm just over the moon he's alive,' William's mother was quoted in Australian media as saying Image: Victoria Police/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement An Australian teenager has been found alive after six days missing in dense bushland. Police said 17-year-old William had been camping with a friend in the southeastern state of Victoria, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) east of Melbourne. He got lost after he'd left his friend to go and get some equipment, but didn't return. The friend then called the police and an intense search operation was launched, involving helicopters, special units, as well as volunteers searching the bush each day. The boy was found on Thursday morning during an aerial search near Stoney Creek, public broadcaster ABC reported. Rescuers first spotted a fishing tackle box and then saw the boy sleeping on a rock in a dry riverbed. 'In good spirits and good health' Pictures show the boy shirtless and sunburned. Local media reported that he waved and pumped his fist when he was woken up the sound of the search helicopter. "Flight officers winched down and retrieved Will before bringing him back to the command post to reunite with his mum," police said. "Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health." He was then taken to hospital for monitoring. "I'm just over the moon he's alive," his mother was quoted in Australian media. "He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued." Police said William had spent days walking through the rugged terrain but fell down the side of a riverbed two days ago and then remained there in hopes of being found. "He's never leaving the house again," his mother told local reporters. "He's grounded for life."
